set_title: Phagocyte defects: recurrent bacterial and fungal infections with normal antibodies
stem: A 7-month-old boy has had recurrent bacterial skin infections and severe gingivitis since early infancy. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte counts are normal. Between infections the leukocyte count stays at 42,000/mm3 with 88% neutrophils.
oneliner: 7M + recurrent skin infections + severe gingivitis + normal Ig and lymphocytes + WBC 42,000 (88% neutrophils) between infections → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: CGD does not keep the **neutrophil count at 42,000 between infections**; its neutrophils reach tissue normally
whyNot.B: Chediak-Higashi gives **neutropenia and giant granules**; his count is 42,000 with 88% neutrophils
whyNot.D: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is **mild and usually silent**; it does not cause a persistent count of 42,000
whyNot.E: SCID gives **lymphopenia** with thrush and viral infections; his lymphocyte count is normal

why: Neutrophils need the CD18 integrin to stick to the vessel wall and leave the blood. Without it they stay in the circulation, so the **count is very high even between infections**, while skin and gums get infections that heal poorly and form little pus.

oneliner: 5M + recurrent abscesses + normal immunoglobulins + normal lymphocytes + normal phagocytosis → CGD or MPO deficiency?
ask: Which single finding favours chronic granulomatous disease over myeloperoxidase deficiency?

stem: A 6-year-old boy has had Burkholderia cepacia pneumonia, a liver abscess and now a pulmonary Aspergillus infection. Serum immunoglobulins are normal. In the laboratory his neutrophils ingest Staphylococcus aureus but do not kill it.

oneliner: 9M + recurrent otitis and pneumococcal sinusitis + normal lymphocytes + IgG, IgA and IgM all very low → ?

stem: A 17-year-old boy is admitted with his second episode of meningococcal meningitis in 3 years. He has had no other serious infections. Serum immunoglobulin concentrations and the lymphocyte count are normal.
oneliner: 17M + second meningococcal meningitis + no other infections + normal immunoglobulins + normal lymphocytes → ?

whyNot.B: DiGeorge gives **neonatal hypocalcemia and viral or fungal infections**, not isolated Neisseria

set_title: Hypersensitivity types I to IV
stem: A 23-year-old woman has worn latex gloves daily for 2 years as a nursing assistant. Twenty minutes into a long shift, she has itchy, red, swollen skin on both hands and wrists that stops sharply at the glove line. She has no wheeze, fever or joint pain.
oneliner: 23F + latex gloves for 2 years + itchy red swollen hands to the glove line 20 minutes into a shift → ?
ask: Which hypersensitivity mechanism is most likely?

options.B: Type II (antibody to cell or matrix antigen)

whyNot.B: Type II needs **antibody to a cell-surface or matrix antigen**, with hemolysis, cytopenia or organ damage; she has a skin reaction at the glove line
whyNot.C: Type III peaks **1 to 2 weeks** after exposure with fever and joint pain; hers began 20 minutes into a shift without either
whyNot.D: Direct mast cell activation follows **systemic drugs such as vancomycin, opioids or contrast** and needs no sensitization; her reaction follows 2 years of latex use and stays where latex touched
whyNot.E: Type IV takes **48 to 72 hours**; her reaction began 20 minutes into the shift

why: Same nurse, one change: **minutes instead of days**. Latex-specific IgE on skin mast cells cross-links and releases histamine at once, giving contact urticaria; the same IgE can cause anaphylaxis.

set_title: Reaction during or after a drug or antiserum
stem: A 55-year-old woman with follicular lymphoma is receiving her second rituximab infusion. Forty minutes in, she develops a temperature of 38.6°C with rigors and diffuse myalgia. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg.

ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Anaphylaxis gives **hives, airway swelling or hypotension**; she has fever, rigors and myalgia with a normal blood pressure
whyNot.C: Serum sickness appears **1 to 2 weeks after** a dose; hers began 40 minutes into the infusion
whyNot.D: An Arthus reaction is **local swelling at an injection site** hours later; hers is a systemic reaction during an infusion
whyNot.E: Tumor lysis shows as **high potassium, phosphate and uric acid with kidney injury** over hours to days; she has fever and rigors 40 minutes in

set_title: Transfusion reactions
stem: A 36-year-old man with a history of recurrent sinusitis and giardiasis receives fresh frozen plasma. Within minutes he has wheezing, abdominal cramps and blood pressure of 78/40 mm Hg. He has no fever.
oneliner: 36M + recurrent sinusitis and Giardia + plasma transfusion + wheeze, cramps, BP 78/40 within minutes + no fever → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: An acute hemolytic reaction brings **fever, flank pain and red urine**; he has none of these and no fever
whyNot.B: A delayed reaction appears **days later** with jaundice; his began within minutes
whyNot.C: An allergic urticarial reaction gives **only hives and itching**; he has wheeze and shock
whyNot.D: TRALI causes **bilateral lung infiltrates and fever within hours**; he has wheeze and cramps within minutes

why: Recurrent sinusitis and Giardia suggest **selective IgA deficiency**. Plasma contains donor IgA, which **anti-IgA antibodies in the recipient** attack, causing anaphylaxis. Use washed cells or IgA-deficient donor products.

set_title: Transplant rejection and GVHD
stem: A 46-year-old man whose first kidney graft failed receives a second kidney from a deceased donor. Within 30 minutes of the vascular clamps being released, the graft swells and stops making urine. Biopsy shows neutrophils in glomerular and peritubular capillaries with fibrin thrombi in arterioles.
oneliner: 46M + second kidney graft + graft swells and stops making urine within 30 min + neutrophils and fibrin thrombi in capillaries → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Acute cellular rejection needs **weeks** for recipient T cells to be primed and invade, and shows lymphocytes in tubules; this graft failed in 30 minutes with neutrophils and thrombi
whyNot.B: Acute antibody-mediated rejection appears **days to weeks** after surgery; this graft failed within 30 minutes of reperfusion
whyNot.C: Chronic rejection is **years** of slow fibrosis and intimal thickening; this graft failed within 30 minutes
whyNot.E: GVHD follows **marrow or stem cell** transplant and attacks host skin, gut and liver; this is a kidney graft failing on the operating table

why: His failed first graft sensitized him, so antibody against donor HLA was **already present before surgery**. It binds graft endothelium as soon as blood flows and fixes complement, causing **thrombosis within minutes**; hence neutrophils and fibrin thrombi in the capillaries.

set_title: Transplant rejection and GVHD
stem: A 29-year-old man receives a kidney from a deceased donor. Eight weeks later he has a tender graft and creatinine has risen from 1.3 to 2.2 mg/dL. Biopsy shows lymphocytes invading the tubular epithelium and the walls of small arteries; staining for C4d in peritubular capillaries is negative.

ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Hyperacute rejection happens in **minutes to hours** with neutrophils and thrombi; this graft worked for 8 weeks
whyNot.C: Antibody-mediated rejection shows **C4d in peritubular capillaries**; his stain is negative and the infiltrate is lymphocytes in tubules
whyNot.D: Chronic rejection is **years** of intimal thickening and fibrosis, not a rapid creatinine rise at 8 weeks
whyNot.E: GVHD needs **donor T cells in the host**; he received a solid organ and the damaged tissue is the graft itself

why: Weeks after surgery, recipient T cells recognize donor MHC and infiltrate the graft. **Lymphocytes in the tubules and arterial walls with no C4d** is the pattern of T cell-mediated rejection; it is treated by boosting immunosuppression.

set_title: Transplant rejection and GVHD
stem: A 38-year-old woman has a kidney transplant. Six weeks later she has oliguria, a tender graft and creatinine rising over several days. Two rejection types are being considered: T cell-mediated and antibody-mediated.
oneliner: 38F + kidney graft 6 weeks ago + oliguria + tender graft + rising creatinine → antibody-mediated or T cell-mediated?
ask: Which single finding favours antibody-mediated rejection over acute cellular rejection?

options.B: Graft tenderness with reduced urine output
options.D: Interstitial edema with scattered mononuclear cells
options.E: Onset in the first weeks after transplant

whyNot.B: Graft swelling and oliguria occur in **both** forms of acute rejection
whyNot.D: Mononuclear cells and edema are seen with **either** type; only **tubulitis** would lean toward cellular

set_title: Transplant rejection and GVHD
stem: A 41-year-old woman received a kidney from a deceased donor 6 years ago. Over 18 months her creatinine has crept from 1.4 to 2.6 mg/dL with new hypertension and 1+ proteinuria. Biopsy shows narrowed arteries with concentric intimal thickening, interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, with little active inflammation.

ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Hyperacute rejection occurs within **minutes to hours**; her graft worked for 6 years

whyNot.D: Antibody-mediated rejection is **acute with C4d capillaritis**; her biopsy shows chronic scarring

set_title: Connective tissue diseases: the deciding autoantibody
stem: A 24-year-old woman has 3 months of fever, painful swollen wrists and pleuritic chest pain. She has an erythematous facial rash over the cheeks and nose that spares the nasolabial folds. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein and red cell casts, and serum anti-dsDNA is positive.

ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Diffuse sclerosis gives **anti-Scl-70 and thickened skin**; she has a malar rash and red cell casts
whyNot.C: Sjogren gives **dry eyes and mouth** with anti-Ro/La; she has a malar rash, arthritis and nephritis
whyNot.D: Dermatomyositis gives **proximal weakness with heliotrope rash**; she has no weakness and a malar rash
whyNot.E: CREST gives **anticentromere with calcinosis and dysmotility**; she has serositis and nephritis instead

why: A malar rash that spares the folds, arthritis, serositis and **glomerulonephritis with anti-dsDNA** is lupus. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific, and anti-dsDNA titers track nephritis.

set_title: Vasculitis: vessel size, lungs and serology
stem: A 43-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B has 3 weeks of fever, abdominal pain after meals, weight loss and a new right foot drop. Blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg, lungs are clear, and ANCA testing is negative. A biopsy of a muscle artery shows segmental transmural necrosis with inflammation of different ages.

ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: GPA involves the **sinuses and lungs** and is c-ANCA positive; his lungs are clear and ANCA negative
whyNot.B: EGPA involves the **lungs, with asthma and eosinophilia**, and is often p-ANCA positive; his lungs are clear and ANCA is negative
whyNot.D: IgA vasculitis is **small-vessel palpable purpura** with abdominal pain, mostly in children; this is a medium-artery biopsy

whyNot.D: Antithrombin deficiency has a **normal baseline aPTT**; hers is prolonged without heparin

why: Clots plus **recurrent fetal loss with a prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing** show an inhibitor, the lupus anticoagulant. In vivo it is **prothrombotic**; in the test tube it blocks the phospholipid in the aPTT reagent.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has a deep vein thrombosis and a prior second-trimester stillbirth. Antiphospholipid syndrome and factor V Leiden are both considered.
oneliner: 27F + DVT + prior stillbirth → antiphospholipid syndrome or factor V Leiden?
ask: Which single finding favours antiphospholipid syndrome over factor V Leiden?

options.A: Deep vein thrombosis of the leg
options.D: Oral contraceptive use as a precipitant
options.E: Prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing with normal plasma

whyNot.A: Venous clots occur in **both**
whyNot.B: Pulmonary embolism is a **venous clot complication** common to both
whyNot.C: The PT is **normal in both** conditions
whyNot.D: Estrogen **precipitates clots in both**, and especially in factor V Leiden

answer: Prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing with normal plasma
why: The **lupus anticoagulant** prolongs the aPTT in the tube while promoting clotting in the body, and mixing does not correct it. Factor V Leiden keeps the **aPTT normal** (it is resistance to activated protein C).

set_title: Shock: which type from the hemodynamics
stem: A 34-year-old woman develops hives, lip swelling, wheezing and lightheadedness 10 minutes after a bee sting. Blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg and pulse is 128/min. Her skin is warm and flushed.
oneliner: 34F + hives, lip swelling, wheeze 10 min after a bee sting + BP 76/40 + pulse 128 + warm flushed skin → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely type of shock?

whyNot.A: Septic shock needs **infection and fever**; she became ill 10 minutes after a bee sting
whyNot.B: Hemorrhagic shock gives **cool pale skin** after blood loss; she has hives and warm flushed skin
whyNot.D: Neurogenic shock follows **cord injury with a slow pulse**; she has no injury and her pulse is 128/min
whyNot.E: Cardiogenic shock follows **MI with raised neck veins**; she has hives and wheeze

why: Hives, angioedema and wheeze minutes after an allergen mean IgE-mediated mast-cell release. **Histamine dilates vessels and leaks plasma**, causing distributive shock with low SVR.

set_title: Blood in the urine with red cell casts: which nephritis
stem: A 24-year-old woman has dark urine and ankle swelling. Blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts and 3+ protein, and serum C3 is low. Lupus nephritis and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis are both being considered.
oneliner: 24F + dark urine + ankle swelling + BP 148/94 + RBC casts + 3+ protein + low C3 → lupus nephritis or poststreptococcal GN?
ask: Which single finding favours lupus nephritis over poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?

options.A: A serum C3 concentration below the reference range
options.B: Red blood cell casts in the urine sediment
options.D: Blood pressure above the reference range
options.E: Protein in the urine on dipstick testing

whyNot.A: **Low C3** occurs in both, because both consume complement
whyNot.B: **Red blood cell casts** show glomerular bleeding in both
whyNot.D: **Hypertension** from salt and water retention occurs in both
whyNot.E: **Proteinuria** occurs in both, as both damage the filtration barrier

why: Both are nephritic syndromes with a low C3. Lupus immune complexes activate the classical pathway, which uses C1, C4 and C2 before C3, so **C4 is low as well**. In poststreptococcal disease the alternative pathway is mainly involved, so C4 stays normal.

set_title: Runny nose, sore throat or fever with cough: which virus, or not an infection at all
stem: A 29-year-old woman has had 2 days of runny nose, sneezing and a scratchy throat. Her temperature is 36.9 C, and she takes no medications. She has had the same symptoms every April for the past 5 years.
oneliner: 29F + 2 days of runny nose + sneezing + scratchy throat + temperature 36.9 C + no medications + same symptoms every April for 5 years → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Rhinitis medicamentosa follows days of decongestant spray; she **takes no medications**
whyNot.B: Adenovirus causes fever with sore throat and red eyes; she is **afebrile at 36.9 C**
whyNot.C: Colds are caught from contacts and do not return on a calendar; hers come back **every April**
whyNot.D: Influenza begins abruptly with fever and severe muscle aches; her temperature is **36.9 C**

set_title: Pneumonia after a transplant or with AIDS: which opportunist, or the graft
stem: A 45-year-old woman has had fever and malaise for 5 days, 3 months after a kidney transplant. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. Cytomegalovirus infection and acute rejection are both being considered.
oneliner: 45F + fever and malaise for 5 days + kidney transplant 3 months ago → cytomegalovirus infection or acute rejection?
ask: Which single finding favours acute rejection over cytomegalovirus infection?

options.A: Fever and malaise that began a few days before presentation
options.B: Tubular epithelium infiltrated by lymphocytes on biopsy
options.C: Lifelong need for immunosuppression to protect the graft
options.D: Onset of illness within the first 6 months after transplant
options.E: A kidney graft that came from a deceased donor

whyNot.A: **Fever and malaise** can come with viral infection or rejection
whyNot.C: **Lifelong immunosuppression** is needed in every recipient, whatever the complication
whyNot.D: Both cytomegalovirus and acute rejection are most common in the **first months** after transplant
whyNot.E: The **donor source** does not separate infection from rejection

answer: Tubular epithelium infiltrated by lymphocytes on biopsy
why: Both occur in the first months under immunosuppression. In acute cellular rejection, T cells attack the graft, so **biopsy shows lymphocytes infiltrating the tubules and vessel walls**. Cytomegalovirus shows owl-eye inclusions instead.
